demos.objective: Recognize how data is organized in everyday situations
demos.slide: syn-s02: slide 2 of 7; slide 2 of 3 in seg-01
demos.chunks:
[syn-s02-c1] (syn-s02) Outline | - Organizing data | - Object basics
[syn-p01-c1] (reference) People organize information all the time so it is quick to use. A music playlist keeps songs in a chosen order. People waiting at a bus stop board in the order they arrived. The undo button in a text editor removes the most recent change first.
demos.script:
This slide shows two main ideas we’ll cover next. First, how we organize data to make it easy to use. Second, the basics of objects—how they help group related information together.

Think about how you already organize things every day. A music playlist keeps songs in a set order so you can play them quickly. People line up at a bus stop in the order they arrived, so the first person gets on first. Even the undo button in a text editor works the same way—it removes the most recent change first, like peeling off the top layer of a stack.

[syn-s03-c1] (syn-s03) Data Organization Around Us | - Music playlist | - Bus stop line | - Undo button | - Library shelves | - Family tree | - Subway map
[syn-p01-c1] (reference) People organize information all the time so it is quick to use. A music playlist keeps songs in a chosen order. People waiting at a bus stop board in the order they arrived. The undo button in a text editor removes the most recent change first.
[syn-p01-c2] (reference) Libraries shelve books by call number, so a reader can walk to the right shelf instead of checking every book. A family tree shows how relatives are connected across generations. A subway map shows stations and the lines that join them.
demos.script: Look around—we organize data all the time to make things easier to use. A music playlist keeps songs in the order you pick, just like people at a bus stop board in the order they arrived. The undo button in a text editor works the same way, removing the last change first. Libraries put books on shelves by call number so you don’t have to search every book, and a family tree shows how relatives connect across generations. Even a subway map is organized data, showing stations and the lines that link them.

demos.question: Which collection does not allow duplicate items?
demos.options:
A: Bag
B: Set
C: List
D: Stack
demos.misconception: Bag rejects duplicates: Believes a bag keeps only one copy of each item.
demos.chunks:
[syn-s05-c1] (syn-s05) Collections | - Bag | - Set | - List | - Stack | - Queue | - Map
[syn-p03-c2] (reference) A bag holds items in no particular order and allows duplicates. A set holds items in no particular order and does not allow duplicates. A list keeps items in a sequence, and each item has a position.
demos.title: Why a bag allows duplicates
demos.text: A lot of you picked bag, thinking it keeps only one copy of each item. But that’s actually what a set does. The lesson says a bag lets you add the same item over and over—it’s like a shopping bag where you can toss in two identical apples. A set, on the other hand, is more like a club guest list: if your name is already on it, you can’t sign up again.
